title: I2C and SPI Protocols
subtitle: Two-wire vs four-wire protocols — connecting sensors, displays, and EEPROMs
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: Many sensors and peripherals (OLEDs, barometric sensors, IMUs, EEPROMs) need a digital communication protocol more capable than a single GPIO pin but more practical than full UART. You need a standard bus that multiple devices can share.
whyItExists.solution: I2C and SPI are the two dominant short-distance synchronous bus protocols. I2C uses only 2 wires and supports up to 128 devices per bus. SPI uses 4 wires per connection but is 10× faster. Knowing both lets you use virtually any peripheral chip.
whyItExists.whenToUse: I2C: when you have many devices to connect and speed is secondary (IMUs, environmental sensors, OLED displays). SPI: when you need speed (SD card, TFT display, DAC, ADC).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: I2C for distances over 1 metre (noise issues). SPI when you're running out of GPIO pins (each device needs its own SS pin).

explainModes.beginner: I2C is like a single street with many numbered houses (device addresses). Every device on the same two wires gets a unique number so they don't interfere with each other. SPI is faster but needs more wires — one dedicated 'you're selected' wire per device.
explainModes.simple: I2C: master sends the 7-bit address, then reads or writes data. All devices share SDA and SCL wires. SPI: master selects a device by pulling its SS pin LOW, then clocks data simultaneously in both directions on MOSI and MISO.
explainModes.standard: I2C is a half-duplex synchronous protocol running at 100 kHz (standard), 400 kHz (fast), or 1 MHz (fast-plus). It's multi-master capable with arbitration. SPI is full-duplex synchronous, up to 20 MHz on Arduino, with no addressing — chip select (SS) pins determine which device is active.
explainModes.technical: I2C transaction: START condition (SDA HIGH→LOW while SCL HIGH) → 7-bit address + R/W bit → ACK → data bytes → STOP. Wire.h uses a 32-byte transmit/receive buffer. SPI uses shift registers for simultaneous TX/RX. SPI has four modes (CPOL × CPHA) — the data sheet specifies which one.
explainModes.deepDive: I2C pull-up resistors are critical: too high (>10 kΩ) slows edges at high speed; too low (<1 kΩ) causes excessive current. At 400 kHz with 3.3 V, 2.2 kΩ pull-ups are standard. Clock stretching allows slow slaves to hold SCL LOW. SPI clock speed is limited by capacitance and wire length — a 50 Ω series resistor on SCLK damps reflections on longer wires.

content.text: I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) uses just two wires: SDA (data) and SCL (clock). Every device on the bus has a unique 7-bit address (0x00–0x7F), enabling up to 128 devices on a single pair of wires. On Arduino Uno: SDA = A4, SCL = A5. The Wire.h library handles all I2C communication.
The BME280 measures temperature, humidity, and barometric pressure — all via I2C. It is one of the most popular environmental sensors and ships at address 0x76 or 0x77.

Run the I2C scanner sketch whenever you get a new I2C device — it confirms the device is wired correctly and shows its actual address. Many modules have address conflicts (two BME280s both at 0x76): change the address jumper or use a multiplexer (TCA9548A).

SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) uses four wires: MOSI (Master Out Slave In), MISO (Master In Slave Out), SCK (clock), and SS/CS (Slave Select / Chip Select). It's faster than I2C (up to 20 MHz) and full-duplex. Each device needs its own SS pin — 4 devices need 4 extra GPIO pins.

a.name: I2C
a.description: Two-wire: SDA + SCL shared by all devices
strengths: Good for slow sensors (BME280, MPU-6050, OLED)
a.useWhen: Many devices, short distances, speed not critical

b.name: SPI
b.description: Four wires: MOSI + MISO + SCK + 1 SS pin per device
strengths: Required for SD cards, TFT displays
weaknesses: No addressing — GPIO pins for chip select
b.useWhen: High speed needed: SD cards, TFT displays, DACs, ADCs

content.text: I2C requires pull-up resistors on both SDA and SCL (typically 4.7 kΩ to Vcc). Most breakout boards include them, but wiring multiple I2C boards together may add too many pull-ups in parallel, dropping resistance below 1 kΩ and causing signal integrity issues. Remove pull-ups from extra boards if you see corrupted I2C data.

questions.question: How many wires does I2C use to connect multiple devices?
options: 2 wires shared among all devices (SDA + SCL)
questions.explanation: I2C uses just 2 shared wires: SDA (data) and SCL (clock). All devices share these lines, differentiated by their unique 7-bit addresses.

questions.question: When should you choose SPI over I2C?
options: When you have more than 8 devices to connect
When you need high speed (SD cards, TFT displays) and have GPIO pins to spare
When you need fewer wires and slower speed
When the device operates at 3.3 V
questions.explanation: SPI is 10–100× faster than I2C, making it essential for SD cards and TFT displays. The trade-off is a dedicated SS pin per device.

questions.question: You scan the I2C bus and find nothing at any address, though a BME280 is connected. What is the most likely cause?
options: The BME280 is incompatible with Arduino
SDA and/or SCL wires are disconnected or swapped
The Serial Monitor baud rate is wrong
questions.explanation: If the scan finds no devices, the most common cause is a wiring fault: SDA/SCL swapped, missing pull-up resistors, or Vcc/GND reversed. Check connections first.

faq.q: When should I choose SPI over I2C?
faq.a: Use SPI for high-speed devices (SD cards ≥4 MHz, TFT displays ≥10 MHz). Use I2C when you have many slow sensors and few spare GPIO pins. I2C is simpler to wire but slower. For most sensors (BME280, MPU-6050, OLED), I2C is fine.

faq.q: Two of my I2C devices have the same address. How do I use both?
faq.a: Option 1: check the datasheet — many devices have address pins to change to a second address. Option 2: use a TCA9548A I2C multiplexer that provides 8 isolated I2C buses, letting you have 8 devices with identical addresses.

faq.q: What pull-up resistor value should I use for I2C?
faq.a: 4.7 kΩ at 100 kHz (standard mode), 2.2 kΩ at 400 kHz (fast mode), 1 kΩ at 1 MHz (fast-plus). Most breakout boards include 4.7 kΩ pull-ups. Too low a value wastes power; too high causes slow edges at high speed.

usedIn: OLED displays (SSD1306 via I2C or SPI)
examples: Weather station connecting BME280 (I2C 0x76) and SSD1306 OLED (I2C 0x3C) on the same two wires
Data logger writing sensor readings to SD card via SPI at 4 MHz
